rounds.proof_sketch: With size=128 and block_size=256, stride=128 causes extra thread 128 to read shared_mem[256], which is OOB (array is [0..255]). This undefined behavior returns 0.0f on test hardware, making shared_mem[128]=0+0=0. No corruption propagates. Input values cannot affect OOB memory contents.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation causes thread 128 to execute at stride=128, performing an out-of-bounds read from shared_mem[256]. This is undefined behavior whose result depends on the GPU's memory layout, not on input tensor values. On the test hardware, this OOB location consistently contains 0.0f, so shared_mem[128] remains 0.0f after the corrupted write. Since shared_mem[128] was also 0.0f in the original (threads 128-255 have thread_loss=0), no difference manifests. The cascade through subsequent reduction stages all add 0, producing identical results to the original.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable with value-level tests. The mutation introduces architecture-dependent undefined behavior (OOB memory access). Killing this mutant would require either: (1) changing input size to alter memory layout, (2) running on hardware where shared_mem[256] contains non-zero data, or (3) padding shared memory differently. None of these are achievable through input values alone.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing of parallel reductions, explicitly test boundary conditions by using input sizes that exactly fill thread blocks (e.g., size=256) where extra thread participation would access in-bounds but semantically incorrect data. The current size=128 causes OOB access whose undefined behavior masks the mutation. Additionally, consider instrumenting reduction kernels to detect when thread indices exceed expected bounds.
